text: Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIPS) is WTO's IP agreement. All WTO members must comply. Key provisions: minimum 20-year patent term, patents in all technology fields, national treatment (foreigners treated same as nationals), most favored nation (equal treatment across countries). Flexibilities: compulsory licensing, parallel imports, Doha Declaration for public health. India compliant since 2005. For AYUSH: TRIPS sets floor for IP protection but allows policy space for public health and TK protection.

TRIPS Article 27.1: Patents available for inventions in all fields of technology, provided they are new, involve inventive step, capable of industrial application. Article 27.2-3 allows exclusions: inventions contrary to ordre public/morality, diagnostic/therapeutic/surgical methods (optional), plants/animals other than micro-organisms (optional). India uses Article 27.3(b) flexibility to exclude plants/animals under Section 3(j). For AYUSH: TRIPS permits but doesn't mandate patenting of medicinal plants.

Doha Declaration on TRIPS and Public Health (2001) affirmed: 1) TRIPS should not prevent members from protecting public health. 2) Flexibilities include compulsory licensing. 3) Each member free to determine grounds for compulsory license. 4) Each member can define 'national emergency'. 5) LDCs given extended transition periods. Waiver for export CL to countries without manufacturing capacity (Article 31bis). For AYUSH: supports India's compulsory licensing provisions and public health-oriented IP policy.

Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property (1883, India member since 1998). Key provisions: 1) National treatment — foreigners get same protection as nationals. 2) Priority right — 12 months to file in other member countries claiming priority. 3) Independence of patents — each country's patent independent. For AYUSH: file in India, then within 12 months file in other Paris Convention countries claiming Indian priority date. Enables international filing strategy.

PCT (1970, India member since 1998) simplifies international patent filing. Single international application filed with WIPO designates multiple countries. Provides: international search report (ISR), optional preliminary examination. National/regional phase entry within 30/31 months. Not a 'world patent' — must enter each country's national phase. Advantages: defer costs, unified search, strategic flexibility. For AYUSH exporters: file PCT, wait for ISR to assess patentability, then enter key markets.

CBD (1992, India ratified 1994) — conservation, sustainable use, benefit sharing from biological resources. Key articles: Article 15 — access to genetic resources subject to prior informed consent (PIC) and mutually agreed terms (MAT). Article 8(j) — protect traditional knowledge, benefit sharing with communities. CBD doesn't itself create enforceable IP rights but influences national laws. India's Biological Diversity Act 2002 implements CBD. For AYUSH: CBD is foundation for NBA approval requirements.

Nagoya Protocol (2010, India ratified 2012) operationalizes CBD's access and benefit sharing (ABS). Key provisions: 1) Provider country establishes access measures. 2) User country ensures compliance by its nationals. 3) Prior informed consent (PIC) from provider. 4) Mutually agreed terms (MAT) for benefit sharing. 5) Internationally recognized certificate of compliance (IRCC). India's NBA approval serves as IRCC. For AYUSH: Nagoya creates international framework — exporting countries may require proof of legal sourcing from India.

WIPO-administered treaties relevant to AYUSH: 1) PCT — international patent filing. 2) Madrid Protocol — international trademark registration. 3) Hague Agreement — international design registration (India not yet member). 4) Budapest Treaty — micro-organism deposit for patents. 5) PLT (Patent Law Treaty) — harmonizes formalities. India is member of PCT, Madrid, Budapest. WIPO also provides IP services, databases, training. For AYUSH: utilize WIPO services for international IP management.

Madrid Protocol (India member since 2013) enables international trademark registration. Single application through WIPO designates multiple member countries (~130). Advantages: one application, one fee, one renewal, centralized management. Process: file through Indian TM Registry, WIPO sends to designated countries, each examines under local law. For AYUSH brands: protect trademarks in multiple export markets through single Madrid filing, significant cost savings vs direct national filings.

Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works (1886, India member since 1928). Key provisions: 1) Automatic protection — no formalities required. 2) National treatment. 3) Minimum terms — life + 50 years (India gives life + 60). 4) Moral rights protection. Covers: literary, artistic, musical, dramatic works. For AYUSH: research papers, product manuals, marketing materials, photographs automatically protected under Berne in all member countries (180+).

International frameworks for traditional knowledge protection: 1) WIPO IGC — negotiations on TK, traditional cultural expressions, genetic resources (ongoing, no treaty yet). 2) CBD/Nagoya — ABS framework for genetic resources and associated TK. 3) UN Declaration on Rights of Indigenous Peoples — recognizes TK rights. 4) FAO International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources — farmers' rights. Gap: no binding international treaty specifically protecting TK as IP. India's TKDL and BD Act are national defensive measures. For AYUSH: rely on national laws and bilateral agreements for TK protection.

UPOV (International Union for Protection of New Varieties of Plants) — India is NOT a member. UPOV provides plant variety protection with breeders' rights but limited farmers' rights. India's PPVFR Act provides stronger farmers' rights (seed saving, sharing) than UPOV allows. Consequence: India can't use UPOV's expedited procedures; must file directly in each country for PVP. For AYUSH: Indian medicinal plant varieties require separate filings internationally.

Bilateral/regional IP agreements affecting AYUSH: 1) India-EU FTA negotiations — IP chapter under discussion. 2) RCEP — India withdrew partly due to IP concerns. 3) Indo-US IP discussions — Watch List concerns. 4) Bilateral investment treaties — may include IP protection. Watch for: TRIPS-plus provisions (data exclusivity, patent term extension), investor-state dispute settlement affecting IP policy. For AYUSH: monitor trade negotiations for IP implications; industry associations often engage in advocacy.

International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (ITPGRFA, 2001, India party). Covers 64 crops for food security (some medicinal plants included). Key: Multilateral System — facilitated access to genetic resources in the system. Standard Material Transfer Agreement (SMTA) — benefit sharing terms. Farmers' Rights recognized (Article 9). For AYUSH: some medicinal crops may be in Multilateral System; check before claiming exclusive rights.
